                    ### Question
                    A 72-year-old man comes to the physician because of several episodes of dark urine over the past 2 months. He has had a 6 kg (13.2-lb) weight loss over the past 3 months despite no changes in appetite. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. A CT scan shows a heterogeneous enhancing mass arising from the left renal pelvis. Pathologic examination of the lesion is most likely to show which of the following findings?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Ulcerating tumor comprised of glandular cells within mucinous material
opb. Pedunculated tumor comprised of pleomorphic urothelial cells with severe nuclear atypia
opc. Tumor with central scar comprised of large eosinophilic cells with central nuclei
opd. Bright yellow tumor comprised of polygonal cells filled with lipids and glycogen
ope. Grayish-tan tumor comprised of primitive blastemal cells forming abortive glomeruli

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 72-year-old man presents with dark urine, weight loss, and a smoking history, which are risk factors for renal cell carcinoma (RCC). The CT scan shows a heterogeneous mass in the left renal pelvis, suggesting a likely diagnosis of transitional cell carcinoma (urothelial carcinoma), which is common in this location. Pathologic examination typically reveals pleomorphic urothelial cells with severe nuclear atypia, aligning with the characteristics of urothelial carcinoma. Other options, such as mucinous glandular cells or lipid-filled cells, are less likely given the presentation and age of the patient. Therefore, the most probable finding in this case is the presence of pleomorphic urothelial cells with severe nuclear atypia.
